question: How does Prati distribute the time between melody, ornament and cadence?
intro: Patrizia Prati played this nocturne at Madrid’s Museum of Romanticism on 24 November 2015. Her live recording offers a second piano account beside Lévy, with its own spacing of melody, ornament and cadence.

sections.mNote: a late swell precedes the final ornamental release

cues.title: Melody over repeated accompaniment
cues.text: Prati’s piano keeps the melodic line distinct from the lower pattern. Listen for the continuity between notes after each attack begins to decay.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies the solo pianist and live performance. The written melody-and-accompaniment texture is described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnes,_Op._9_(Chopin); no individual touch or pedal action is inferred.

cues.title: An early recorded crest
cues.text: The opening span rises and releases into quieter sound. Follow the melodic gesture across its crest instead of treating the strongest attack as a separate event.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 0:44; level rises from −21.6 dB at 0:35 to −12.7 dB at 0:45, then falls to −22.1 dB at 1:00.

cues.title: A broad middle swell
cues.text: This middle stretch sustains its greater weight across several phrases before withdrawing. Listen to the upper line throughout that span, not just its individual high points.
cues.evidence: The 1:30–1:50 windows remain between −11.0 and −8.4 dB; level then falls to −18.6 dB at 1:55, after the 1:52 boundary.

cues.title: Another sustained rise
cues.text: Prati shapes a later rise that continues across several successive gestures. Hear how the music gathers weight before the attacks become more closely spaced.
cues.evidence: The 2:38 boundary is inside a sustained higher-level span at 2:35–3:00. Detected onset density rises from 1.6 at 2:45 to 4.6 per second at 3:00.

cues.title: A quieter later passage
cues.text: The quieter later span provides space before the closing build. Continue following the melody even where the recorded weight is reduced.
cues.evidence: After the 3:22 boundary, level stays around −21 to −18 dB through 3:55, substantially below the later 4:10–4:20 crest within this recording.

cues.title: The closing crest
cues.text: The late build reaches the recording’s strongest span and then sheds weight. The following cluster of attacks is lighter: density and intensity need not rise together.
cues.evidence: The highest windows are 4:10 and 4:15. At 4:30 onset density reaches 5.6 per second while level has dropped to −17.2 dB; the 4:24 boundary locates the change.

cues.title: The final renewal
cues.text: The last cadential sound briefly renews the piano’s resonance before the ending fades. Let the decay complete the close rather than stopping at the final clear attack.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary is 4:40; level rises from −25.3 dB at 4:35 to −17.4 dB at 4:40, then falls to −44.7 dB at 4:55. No new attacks are detected after 4:50.

transitions.title: The phrase starts another ascent
transitions.how: A quieter passage leads into another sustained rise. The piano’s melody-and-accompaniment texture stays in place while phrase weight changes.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 2:26; level rises from −19.9 dB at 2:25 to −8.4 dB at 2:45.

transitions.title: The quieter line gains weight
transitions.how: The subdued late span gathers into the final broad crest. Its release is articulated by lighter, denser attacks before the last cadence.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 3:56 precedes the rise to the 4:10–4:20 crest; the later 4:30 window has increased attack density and reduced level.

transitions.title: The last sound is renewed
transitions.how: The ornamental release gives way to the final cadential sound, renewing the resonance before the piano falls silent. Harmonic arrival precedes the disappearance of the sound.
transitions.evidence: The written work closes in E♭ major. The strong 4:40 boundary and renewed level precede decay through 4:50–5:00; the exact score bar is not aligned here.

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
